opus-5.5.text:
I think you have a pretty serious responsibility, honestly more than when you're writing a paper about your own method. When you criticize someone else's work, you're making a claim about people who aren't in the room, and those people usually have less of a voice in that moment than you do. So the first obligation is to get it right. You need to be at least as rigorous in the critique as you're asking them to have been in the original work. A sloppy paper complaining about sloppiness is the worst of all worlds.

The second thing is to criticize the work, not the people. It's very easy, especially in machine learning where things move fast and there's a lot of hype, to slide into a tone that implies the original authors were careless or acting in bad faith. In almost every case they weren't. They were working under the same incentives we all work under: deadlines, reviewers who want state-of-the-art numbers, limited compute. If there's a problem, it's often a problem with the field's norms more than with any individual paper, and I think the critique should be framed that way.

Third, I think you owe the original authors a conversation. Where possible, reach out before you publish. Tell them what you found and give them a chance to respond. Sometimes you find out you misunderstood something, or there's a detail that wasn't in the paper. Sometimes they agree with you and that's great. Either way the final product is better and fairer.

And finally, I think you have a responsibility to be constructive. It's not enough to say "this evaluation is broken." You should try to say what a better evaluation looks like, or at least what questions people should be asking. The goal isn't to win an argument. It's to help the field figure out what's actually true, and ideally the people whose work you're critiquing come away feeling like you've helped them too, even if it stung a little.

I'll admit I haven't always lived up to all of that perfectly. But it's the standard I try to hold myself to, because I'd want the same courtesy if someone were writing about my work, and inevitably someone will be.

r001.rationale: The response says critiques should be constructive and offer a better evaluation or identify questions people should ask, articulating a path forward.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the first responsibility is to get it right, and that sounds obvious, but it's harder than it sounds. When you're criticizing someone else's work, you have to hold yourself to a higher standard than the work you're criticizing. If I'm going to say that a result doesn't hold up, I need to have run the experiments carefully enough that I'd be comfortable if the original authors came and looked over my shoulder. Because they will. And they should.

The second thing, and I feel strongly about this, is that you have a responsibility to be criticizing the science and not the people. These are real humans who put a lot of work into what they did, usually in good faith. The lottery ticket work got a lot of scrutiny, some of it from people who found real limitations, and the pieces of that criticism that I found most useful were the ones that engaged with the ideas and left me out of it. When I've written things that push back on other results, I've tried to do the same. The goal isn't to score a point, it's to make the field's understanding more accurate, and you can do that without making anyone feel attacked.

Third, I think you owe people a conversation before you owe them a paper. If I have a result that contradicts something, I should reach out to the authors first. Sometimes they'll tell me I misread the setup, or there's a hyperparameter I missed, and I'd much rather learn that in an email than after I've put something on arXiv. And sometimes they'll say, yeah, we've been wondering about that too. That kind of exchange makes the eventual paper better and it's just the decent thing to do.

And then the last piece is being honest about what the criticism actually shows. There's a temptation to say "this doesn't work" when what you've actually shown is "this doesn't work in this setting at this scale with these choices." Those are very different claims. Our field moves fast and people read abstracts, so if you overclaim in a critique, you can do real damage to a line of work that might have been fine. I've tried to be careful to say precisely what we found and no more, even when the stronger statement would get more attention.

r001.rationale: The response stresses accuracy, fair criticism, author conversations, and avoiding overclaims, but does not say critics have a responsibility to articulate a constructive path forward.

astra-6.text:
I think you have a responsibility to be very careful, because you’re talking about work that somebody put a lot of time and thought into. You should hold your criticism to at least the same standard of evidence that you’re asking of the original paper. And you should be precise about what you’ve actually shown. There’s a big difference between saying, “We couldn’t reproduce this result,” and saying, “This result is wrong.”

I also think you should give the authors a chance to respond before you publish. Maybe you misunderstood something. Maybe there’s a detail you missed. That doesn’t mean they get a veto over your conclusions, but you want to make sure you’re criticizing the strongest, most accurate version of their work.

Ultimately, the goal should be to help us understand something better. And you can be direct—even very critical—while still treating the people involved with respect.

r001.rationale: The response says criticism should help improve understanding, but it does not state a responsibility to articulate a constructive path forward.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have a responsibility to be incredibly careful. If you’re going to criticize someone’s work, you need to understand what they actually claimed, make a good-faith effort to reproduce it, and be clear about what your evidence does and doesn’t show. There’s a big difference between “I couldn’t get this to work” and “this doesn’t work.”

And I think you should talk to the authors. Give them a chance to point out something you missed. The goal should be to help us understand the science better, and that includes being willing to discover that your criticism was wrong.

r001.rationale: The response calls for careful, good-faith criticism and dialogue with authors, but does not state that critics should articulate a constructive path forward.
